claims.text: Cold spray deposition using Ni-Al alloy powder can rebuild a damaged nickel-based superalloy surface.
The Ni-Al cold-spray deposit can reinforce the superalloy surface.
Cold spraying under the proposed conditions produces a refined, densely consolidated coating.
The deposited coating contains work-hardened regions.
Cold spraying provides strong mechanical interlocking between the Ni-Al deposit and the nickel-based superalloy substrate.
High-velocity particle impact induces severe plastic deformation.
High-velocity particle impact induces adiabatic shear.
Severe plastic deformation and adiabatic shear lead to grain refinement in the deposit.
Cold-spray bonding and mechanical interlocking occur without the material reaching its melting temperature.
Avoiding melting and limiting thermal exposure reduce hot-cracking risk relative to traditional fusion-welding repair.
The cold-sprayed surface has greater hardness than both a fusion-welded repair and an untreated damaged surface.
The cold-sprayed surface has greater wear resistance than both a fusion-welded repair and an untreated damaged surface.
The cold-sprayed surface has greater corrosion resistance than both a fusion-welded repair and an untreated damaged surface.
Particle velocities of 600-900 m/s are an operative processing range for the proposed repair.
The proposed repair can be performed with the substrate maintained near room temperature.
The proposed repair can be performed either in ambient atmosphere or under inert-gas protection.
Insufficient deposit-substrate bonding may cause premature delamination or suboptimal repair performance.
Surface pretreatment or graded-powder strategies may improve inadequate interfacial bonding.

contradictions.description: The structural mediator says the coating ensures strong mechanical interlocking, whereas the uncertainty field states that bonding and consolidation may be insufficient and could cause premature delamination.
